name: A database
description: Rows and tables in a SQL database such as Postgres, MySQL or SQL Server.

objects.label: rows
objects.description: Rows of a table or view. Filter by column name.

objects.label: tables
objects.description: The tables and views in the database, with a rough row count.

fields.label: number of rows
fields.description: An estimate from the database's statistics, not an exact count.

fields.label: last updated
fields.description: When a row was last inserted or changed, if the database tracks it.

actions.label: new rows
actions.description: One new row per record. Existing rows are left alone.

params.label: with the columns
params.description: Leave empty to write every field whose name matches a column.

actions.label: updates to existing rows
actions.description: Changes the matching rows in place. Rows that do not match are not created.

params.label: matched on
params.description: The column that identifies the row, usually the ID or primary key.

guidance: A database is reached over its native driver (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server and so on) with a login made for the automation, normally against a read replica or a view rather than the primary. Name the schema, table and columns exactly as they appear in the database; some engines are case-sensitive and a wrong name fails only at run time. Ask for a read-only login for reading and a separate login limited to INSERT or UPDATE on the named tables for writing, and never reuse an application's own credentials.

setup.notes: The DBA or the team that owns the application knows which database, schema and login to use. They will usually want to see the exact query before granting access.
